The Work, Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas: Studies in His Life, His Book "Reishit Chochmah" and the Moral Kabbalah of Safed and Hebron
His Life, Historical Background and the Move from Safed to Hebron
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas (5276 – 5347; approximately 1518–1587) was active during the 16th century, a period of spiritual and kabbalistic flourishing in the Land of Israel under Ottoman rule [cite: 1, 2]. He was born in the city of Safed to a distinguished family of Iberian Peninsula origin, which had relocated to the Land of Israel in the wake of the Expulsion from Spain [cite: 1]. In his youth he was orphaned of his father, Rabbi Moshe de Vidas, and experienced childhood and young-adult years marked by material hardship and suffering [cite: 1]. These living conditions contributed to shaping his temperament, which was characterized by asceticism, exceptional humility and total devotion to spiritual service [cite: 1]. Rabbi Eliyahu was also the brother-in-law of Rabbi Shalom HaKohen, the head of the rabbinic court (av beit din) of Safed [cite: 3].
During the first half of the 16th century Safed served as the world center of the esoteric lore, in which eminent sages and kabbalists gathered. Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas grew up within this spiritual climate, in which mysticism was fused with social and personal practices of rectifying the soul [cite: 3, 4, 5]. However, in the wake of the economic and political decline of the Jewish community of Safed in the second half of the 16th century, Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas moved south and settled in the city of Hebron [cite: 1, 3, 6].
In 5326 (1566) Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas was appointed head of the rabbis of Hebron and led the spiritual and halakhic life of the community in the city [cite: 1, 3, 6]. His move to Hebron marked the beginning of the city's transformation into a major kabbalistic center in the Land of Israel, which attracted students and kabbalists [cite: 2, 7]. In Hebron he completed the work of his literary life, the book "Reishit Chochmah," whose completion is noted with the date 18 Adar 5335 (1575) [cite: 1, 8].
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas passed away in Hebron in 5347 (1587) and was buried in the ancient cemetery of the city, in a plot that was afterwards given the name "Sde Reishit Chochmah" or the rabbis' plot [cite: 3, 6, 9]. His grave became a focus of pilgrimage throughout the generations, as travelers and rabbis attest, among them Aharon ben Menachem Mendel of Kamenitz in his book "Korot HaItim" (1839) [cite: 2]. The tent built over his grave at the beginning of the 20th century was destroyed during the period of Jordanian rule after the riots of 5689, and was afterwards restored and rebuilt by Prof. Ben-Zion Tavger as part of the rehabilitation of the ancient cemetery [cite: 1, 3].
His Teachers, His Spiritual Circle and His Kabbalistic Development
The thought and spirituality of Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas were shaped under the direct influence of the greatest kabbalists of Safed, the central and most influential figure on his path being his foremost teacher, Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak) [cite: 2, 3, 4]. Rabbi Eliyahu consistently calls the Ramak by the title "my teacher" in his writings, and upon the Ramak's death in 5330 (1570) his manuscripts were entrusted to him [cite: 1, 3]. The spiritual bond between the Ramak and de Vidas was so deep that Rabbi Chaim Vital and the kabbalists of the generation regarded their souls as stemming from one soul-root [cite: 10]. In the kabbalistic tradition of "Likutei Torah" it is cited in the name of the Ari that the soul of the Ramak and the soul of Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas are a reincarnation of the soul of Benaiah ben Jehoiada, which was reincarnated in Zechariah the prophet, split into Shemaiah and Avtalyon, and finally reached them [cite: 3].
Alongside his study with the Ramak, Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas was also counted among the circle of students of Rabbi Yitzchak Luria (the Ari) [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Although his basic teaching rests on Cordoverian Kabbalah, he knew the Ari's innovations, calls him "my teacher" in some of his writings, and statements in his name were cited in the writings of the Ari's disciples, such as the book "Shaar Ruach HaKodesh" by Rabbi Chaim Vital [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Another important teacher of his was Rabbi Avraham HaLevi Berukhim (the Maghrebi), one of the great ascetics (perushim) of Safed, known for his laments over the destruction of the Temple and for his night tikkunim [cite: 1, 3]. The practical figure of Rabbi Avraham HaLevi left a strong mark on de Vidas's writing with regard to mourning over the exile of the Shekhinah and the realization of moral conduct [cite: 1, 3].
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas was part of the "Fellowship of Kabbalists" of Safed, which included the Ramak, Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz and other sages [cite: 1, 3]. The fellowship used to go out for solitary meditation and Torah study in the fields and mountains surrounding Safed [cite: 1, 3]. This practice was called by them "gerushin" (banishment), and it was perceived as active participation in the exile of the Shekhinah and as a tool for creating mystical inspiration and the revelation of the secrets of the Torah [cite: 1, 3]. In addition, his moral teaching was deeply influenced by the writings of the early kabbalist Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, from whom he adopted ecstatic motifs and a broad emphasis on devekut (cleaving to God), solitary meditation and the binding of thought to God [cite: 1].
The Corpus of Writings: "Reishit Chochmah" and Related Literature
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas's central work is the book Reishit Chochmah, regarded as one of the cornerstones of kabbalistic moral literature [cite: 4, 11, 12]. The name of the book derives from the verse in Psalms: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord" (Psalms 111:10) [cite: 8, 12, 13]. The book was first printed in Venice in 5338 (1578) by his nephew, Rabbi Eliezer HaKohen, and since then it has been printed in more than fifty editions, has received many adaptations and abridgements, and has been accepted in all the communities of Israel [cite: 1, 4, 14].
The book is structured in a comprehensive format of five central gates, which describe the spiritual qualities (middot) that a person must perfect, alongside appended sections detailing the application of the qualities in everyday life [cite: 4].
Part / Gate in the book | Main content and conceptual focus | Sources and methodological approach
Gate of Fear | Clarifying the essence of the fear of the Lord, distinguishing between fear of punishment and fear of exaltation, and describing the punishments of Gehinnom and the transmigrations of the soul [cite: 4]. | Analysis of the statements of the holy Zohar, integration of the warnings of the Sages, and laying the foundations for the soul's longing for its source [cite: 4].
Gate of Love | Cultivating love of the holy Lord, attaining devekut, self-sacrifice and the intention of the commandments [cite: 4, 15]. | Integration of the ecstatic conceptions of Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre and a commentary on the Song of Songs in the esoteric manner [cite: 1, 15].
Gate of Repentance | Paths of rectification, confession, uprooting sin, fasts, and the order of rectifying the blemishes of the soul and of the sefirot [cite: 4]. | Practical guidance for kabbalistic repentance, based on the connection between a person's transgressions and the blemish in the upper worlds [cite: 4, 11].
Gate of Holiness | Guarding the senses, the holiness of thought, purity of the body, the conduct of eating, and the conduct of the household and marital union [cite: 4, 16]. | Detailed moral-physical instructions (including chapters 15–17, devoted to family purity) [cite: 4, 16].
Gate of Humility | The root of all good qualities, negation of the ego, distancing pride and subduing materiality [cite: 4]. | Presenting humility as the only receptacle for causing the Shekhinah to dwell and for attaining hidden wisdom [cite: 4, 11].
Chapter on the Commandments and Chapter on Derekh Eretz | Applying morality in practical life: conducting business faithfully, social fairness, human relations and derekh eretz [cite: 4, 12]. | Bringing statements of the Sages and emphasizing that social integrity and good qualities take precedence over mystical attainments [cite: 4, 12].
Chuppat Eliyahu Rabbah | A moral repository and statements of the Sages arranged in numerical order (statements of three things, four, and so on) [cite: 4, 17]. | An expanded collection from midrashim, tractate Avot and the literature of the Sages to strengthen the work on the qualities [cite: 4, 17].
Or Olam / Or Gadol | Statements of encouragement, intentions of prayer and further kabbalistic collections [cite: 4]. | A kabbalistic-moral closing piece intended to complete the learner's general worldview [cite: 4].
Besides the book "Reishit Chochmah," Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas left further works and adaptations intended for the general public:
Totzaot Chaim: a popular abridgement of the book "Reishit Chochmah," composed in order to enable every person to study its main teachings daily [cite: 1, 3]. The book includes condensed moral instructions, intentions of prayer and brief commentaries [cite: 3, 18].
Michtav Eliyahu: a moral-kabbalistic work dealing with the rectification of the qualities and with devekut [cite: 3, 6].
Or Olam (Kavanat HaShem): a kabbalistic work devoted to unifications, the intentions of the holy names and the secrets of prayer [cite: 3, 6].
His Moral and Kabbalistic Teaching: Fundamental Principles
The teaching of Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas represents the peak of the branch of kabbalistic moral thought that grew in Safed. Whereas in earlier periods Kabbalah was studied as a cosmological theory intended only for chosen individuals, de Vidas – following his teacher the Ramak in his book "Tomer Devorah" – fused kabbalistic mysticism with the world of morality and everyday practice [cite: 2, 4, 11, 19]. According to his approach, Kabbalah is not merely a wisdom for understanding the Divinity, but practical guidance for refining the human being and repairing the world [cite: 4, 12, 15].
This conception rests on a deep foundation of ontological continuity between the Divinity and the human being, known as the doctrine of the double soul [cite: 5]. According to de Vidas, the human soul is not severed from its upper sources; there is an inherent and unbroken connection linking the divine Infinite (Ein Sof) with the human soul clothed in the physical body [cite: 5]. Through his interpretation of the verse "For the portion of the Lord is His people, Jacob the lot of His inheritance" (Deuteronomy 32:9), de Vidas explains that the bond between the human being and the Creator is illustrated by the image of the rope: its upper end is anchored in the upper root of the soul in the Divinity, while its lower end extends into this world [cite: 5, 20]. As a result, every deed, utterance or bad quality of a person below damages the flow of divine abundance in the upper worlds, whereas the rectification of the qualities, holiness and the study of Torah draw spiritual abundance from the depths of the Divinity into physical reality [cite: 5, 15].
In addition, de Vidas incorporated into his book meditative instructions originating in the book of the Zohar and in the writings of Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre [cite: 1, 12, 14]. The learner is required to visualize the letters of the Holy Tongue, to contemplate combinations of holy names and to direct his thought to purify the powers of the soul [cite: 12, 14, 21]. The aim of this practice is to strip thought of the shackles of matter and to bring the person to the level of constant devekut [cite: 12, 15].
In de Vidas's teaching, the rectification of personal qualities is not intended only to save the soul from punishment, but constitutes an integral part of the cosmic and universal rectification [cite: 15]. The rectification of the individual's qualities participates actively in the redemption of the Shekhinah from its exile, in the raising of the fallen holy sparks, and in the union of the upper sefirot [cite: 3, 15]. Sages of the generations testified that Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas fulfilled in his body and in his way of life everything that he wrote and taught in his book; this was stated explicitly by Rabbi Chaim Palagi in the introduction to his book "Tokhachat Chaim" and by Rabbi Yechezkel Shraga Halberstam of Shinova in his book "Divrei Yechezkel" [cite: 3].
His Students and His Influence on the Community of Hebron
With the move of Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas to Hebron in 5326 (1566) and his appointment as head of the city's rabbis, the community in Hebron underwent a process of deep spiritual renewal [cite: 1, 3, 6]. He founded in the city a study hall for the study of the revealed and the hidden Torah, and gathered around him a group of students and kabbalists who adopted the practices of asceticism, the tikkunim and the devekut of the sages of Safed [cite: 2, 7].
His influence on the community in Hebron was long-lasting: he laid the foundation for the transformation of Hebron into a central kabbalistic center in the 17th and 18th centuries, from which famous kabbalists and sages later arose [cite: 2, 7]. His presence and the place of his burial in the ancient cemetery of the city made Hebron a protected and sanctified site in Jewish tradition, and were a source of inspiration for generations of sages who were active in the city [cite: 2, 9]. In the rabbis' plot where he was buried, other sages were buried beside him, among them Rabbi Shlomo Adani (author of the commentary "Melekhet Shlomo" on the Mishnah), Rabbi Chizkiyahu Medini (author of "Sdei Chemed") and Rabbi Eliyahu Mani [cite: 9].
His Influence and Legacy for the Generations
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas's book, "Reishit Chochmah," became one of the most influential works in the history of Jewish moral and religious literature and thought, and left a deep mark on central spiritual movements in the centuries since its printing [cite: 4, 11, 22].
Movement / Public | Nature of the influence and use of the work | Practical manifestations and sources
The Hasidic movement | "Reishit Chochmah" served as a canonical foundational book. The Baal Shem Tov and his disciples saw in it a guide to devekut, to joy and to the rectification of the soul [cite: 16, 22]. | Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonne cited it extensively [cite: 6, 22]. The Alter Rebbe of Chabad required daily study of the work as a precondition for studying the book Tanya [cite: 16].
Opposition to Hasidism | Because of the ruling of the Alter Rebbe, some of the Mitnagdic sages decreed a prohibition on studying the book, in order to prevent being drawn after Hasidism [cite: 16]. | Studying the book was regarded as a distinct mark of belonging to the Hasidic sect (as described in the story of Rabbi Avraham Sheines) [cite: 16].
Chabad customs and grooms | The book was studied by the Chabad Rebbes on the two special days of their lives (such as the Lubavitcher Rebbe on his wedding day) [cite: 16]. | An explicit practice for all grooms to study chapters 15, 16 and 17 of the "Gate of Holiness" before the wedding as guidance for a rectified life [cite: 16].
The Lithuanian Mussar movement | The book was accepted as an inalienable asset alongside "Mesillat Yesharim," but the emphasis was placed on the service of fear of God, the breaking of pride and the refinement of the qualities [cite: 23, 24]. | Rabbi Yisrael Salanter and the heads of the yeshivas in Lithuania included "Reishit Chochmah" in the yeshiva study curriculum of the Mussar movement [cite: 23, 24].
East European Jewry and the Sephardim | Wide circulation in all the communities, the printing of many editions, Yiddish translations and popular adaptations [cite: 1, 4, 14]. | The printing of abridgements (such as "Totzaot Chaim") that were studied by laymen and Torah scholars alike [cite: 1, 10, 18].
The extent of the work's influence on the Hasidic movement is underscored by the testimony of the Rebbe (Rashash"z) of Kapust, who confirmed that when the book Tanya was printed in 5556 (1796), the Alter Rebbe (Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi) commanded that whoever does not study the book "Reishit Chochmah" should not study the book Tanya either [cite: 16]. The Alter Rebbe even wrote in his letters: "Let him study Reishit Chochmah every day, for it is full of wisdom and fear of God and of character traits, filled to overflowing" [cite: 16].
This instruction led to a sharp counter-step on the part of Mitnagdic sages, who enacted that the book "Reishit Chochmah" not be studied, as a fence "to safeguard the matter" (le-migdar milta), so as not to be drawn after the Hasidic movement [cite: 16]. A fascinating historical testimony from that period tells of Rabbi Avraham Sheines (son-in-law of the Alter Rebbe), who in his youth was secretly drawn to Hasidism and used to hide the book "Reishit Chochmah" under the pillow of his bed in order to study it quietly before sleep; when his father discovered this, he struck him with his staff in great anger for having been caught studying this book [cite: 16].
In the Mussar movement that arose in the 19th century in Lithuania through Rabbi Yisrael Salanter, the book "Reishit Chochmah" was studied alongside other classic moral books [cite: 23, 24]. However, whereas the Lithuanian Mussar movement focused mainly on the psychological analysis of the soul, on the breaking of the qualities and on turning away from evil, the Hasidic movement adopted from "Reishit Chochmah" the motif of devekut, the contemplation of the greatness of the Creator, and spiritual service out of joy and inner connection [cite: 16, 23].
Conclusions
Rabbi Eliyahu de Vidas is a key figure in the history of Jewish thought and mysticism. His spiritual work successfully bridged the speculative and complex Kabbalah of his teacher the Ramak and of the Ari and the religious and moral world of the general public [cite: 4, 11, 12].
His historical and Torah significance is expressed in three central dimensions:
Democratization of Kabbalah: through his book "Reishit Chochmah," de Vidas extracted the esoteric teaching from the innermost chambers and made it an accessible guide to the work on the qualities, the rectification of character and divine devekut [cite: 4, 12, 15].
Establishing the center of Kabbalah in Hebron: his move from Safed to Hebron and his service as head of the city's rabbis laid the foundations for the growth of Hebron as a first-rate kabbalistic and spiritual center over centuries [cite: 1, 3, 7].
Lasting cross-current influence: his writings crossed geographic and conceptual boundaries and became a shared conceptual infrastructure that nourished the Hasidic movement, the Mussar movement, and the daily practices in the Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities alike [cite: 4, 16, 23, 24].
